items.title: 'A complete surprise' - XDS-Astana respond to Harold Tejada biological passport abnormalities
items.author: Katy Madgwick
items.content:
XDS-Astana have responded to the news that Harold Tejada is under investigation by the International Testing Agency (ITA), following suspected abnormalities in his biological passport.

It was revealed on Friday, November 27, that Netcompany-Ineos had terminated their contract with Tejada following the news that the 29-year-old from Colombia had been notified of an anti-doping rule violation over the alleged use of a prohibited substance or method, following unexplained abnormalities in his biological passport.

Tejada enjoyed success in 2026 at Paris-Nice, winning stage 6, and was second in a stage at the Tour de France, before recording a top-10 finish at the Vuelta a España later in the summer.

He was due to transfer from XDS-Astana to Netcompany-Ineos in January 2027. He remains under contract with XDS-Astana until December 31.

“This came as a complete surprise to the team,” XDS Astana said in a statement also issued on Friday, November 27.

“In accordance with the disciplinary procedure before the ITA/UCI, the rider will be given an opportunity to present his defense and/or to accept the violation and a sanction. The team is not part of these proceedings. It is now for the relevant authorities to assess the case.

“The team has a zero-tolerance policy with respect to doping practices, and it supports the UCI/ITA efforts to fight against doping in the sport of cycling.”

Astana confirmed that Tejada had been suspended from the team, effective immediately.

Tejada has spent his entire professional career at the Kazakh team, turning pro with them in 2020 and remaining for some seven seasons. His results gradually improved, from a stage win at the 2019 Tour de l'Avenir, which underscored his considerable climbing potential, to a victory on home soil at the 2024 Tour of Colombia, and finally his first WorldTour stage win at the 2026 Paris-Nice.

Tejada released a statement on Friday, maintaining his innocence and stating his intention to cooperate with the investigation process. "From day one, I have acted with diligence and responsibility, providing all requested information in a timely manner. I will continue to do so throughout the entire process, with full respect for the anti-doping authorities and cycling institutions."

items.title: Wout van Aert to make cyclo-cross return in Antwerp, with World Championships tilt on the cards
items.author: Katy Madgwick
items.content:
Wout van Aert has confirmed his return to the cyclo-cross field for the 2026-2027 season, with the likely aim of representing Belgium at the UCI World Championships in Ostend in January.

According to Flemish newspaper , the Visma-Lease a Bike rider will make his debut on December 19 in Antwerp, the same place where he began his campaign last season, finishing 7th on the day.

Van Aert raced a reduced calendar of six races in 2025-2026 and, despite two second-place finishes, was unable to record a win in the discipline for the first time since his debut season in 2010. He was set to race eight races in total but an ankle fracture sustained in Mol in early January forced an early end to his winter programme.

This season he looks set to expand his off-road schedule, with the suggestion that he may race around 12 races, with the first indication that these will include the World Championships in Ostend on January 31, 2027, an outcome which Belgian national coach Angelo De Clercq had previously suggested was uncertain.

It's still a relatively late start for Van Aert, as hopes for a potential debut at the Superprestige series in Ruddervoorde were quashed by confirmation that the Belgian would attend Visma-Lease a Bike's Spanish training camp in early December.

While his exact race programme is yet to be determined, it looks increasingly likely that Van Aert will take aim at the world title in January. He had already confirmed he would opt out of the most recent edition in Hulst in 2026 prior to his ankle injury, moving on from the mud to targets on the road, with the Spring Classics his first major goals of the season.

This season could mark a return to Worlds for a tilt at a rainbow jersey that he won three years in a row, from 2016-2018. His three most recent attempts to repeat the feat have resulted in second-place finishes to his long-time rival, Mathieu van der Poel, including in Ostend in 2021. It's currently unclear whether or not the Dutchman intends to race off-road this winter.

As for Van Aert, the 32-year-old has reduced his participation in the off-road discipline where he made his name in recent seasons; however, he continues to include cyclocross as part of his schedule, racing every season since his junior debut in 2010. This season marks his 17th consecutive winter as an elite cyclo-cross rider.

items.title: 'It's always sour to lose' admits Tibor Del Grosso after going second to Thibau Nys in Ostrava at World Cup opener
items.author: Ben Goddard
items.content:
The 23-year-old was battling for victory on the last lap with rival Thibau Nys (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions), but came out second best in the first duel of the season between the pair.

Del Grosso said that he felt ‘sour’ losing to his Belgian rival after conceding the lead and failing to regain the front position in the snow during the final corners, while Nys stayed on the firmer ground.

“I don't think it was a bad performance, if you're close to winning. Of course, it's always sour to lose,” said Del Grosso afterwards to organisers.

“It was just a matter of having the lead and keeping the lead going into the last corner, at some point Thibau [Nys] came with quite some speed. I felt like there were some opportunities after, to still overtake him, but then I waited maybe a bit too long.

“The bit towards the final corner, there was only really one path where you could ride in. I tried to overtake, didn't really go anywhere.”

Del Grosso announced that he will ride 13 races this cyclo-cross season – all of the 12 World Cup rounds and the World Championships in Oostend.

Last season the Dutchman came into his first elite season from the under-23 ranks and finished 14th in his opening race at the World Cup round at Namur in mid-December. Before racing in Ostrava, the 23-year-old joked that a 13th place finish Friday would be an improvement of last year's first race.

“I think a lot of people think about my [cyclo-cross] races from last season,” said Del Grosso. “Last year I also needed some time to get into it. I didn’t prepare to be here in my best shape.”

Del Grosso looked comfortable on the slippery terrain in Ostrava and was able to follow Nys before putting his rival under pressure in the final laps.

“I have mixed feelings, I can be quite happy with my race today. The feeling was not yet where it was supposed to be. It was a really tactical race with how the course was. I think I played it relatively well, but then the final two minutes was not perfect," he reflected.

“I don't think it was a bad performance. Technically, I think it's a good 'cross. Some points for improvement, but also not crazy. A lot better than last year.”

Del Grosso competed on the road this season with Alpecin-Premier Tech and won the NXT Classic in April then adding 14th in Amstel Gold Race. The Dutchman took a two-month break following his last road race in the Flandrien Classic and National Coach Gerben de Knegt believed that it has allowed the youngster to ‘rest and train well’.

He told : "His road season has been somewhat disappointing for various reasons. He rested well and trained well. In other years, he also started the [cyclo-cross] season quite quickly after his road campaign.

“Now he is better prepared because he has been able to train for more weeks between the end of the road season and the start of his cyclo-cross winter.”

items.title: Bad luck for Lucinda Brand with mechanical issues in snowy opening round of cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava
items.author: Ben Goddard
items.content:
The picturesque venue was a step into the unknown, with the Czech Republic hosting its first-ever World Cup event.

While the snow and Christmas lights made for a unique setting at the former coal mine venue, the frozen surface and deep ruts made for dangerous conditions. The evening race saw temperatures drop below freezing, and Brand was one of several casualties of the frozen ground.

At the halfway point, Brand was fighting in the top 10 before she couldn't clip into her pedals, a problem that many riders suffered during the elite women's and elite men's race.

For the Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions rider, though, she was left frustrated and shouting at her pit crew as they desperately tried to solve the issue from the pits.

Brand then lost over a minute and couldn't regain the time in the difficult conditions, finishing 15th and 2:25 behind race winner Marie Schreiber (SD Worx–Protime).

Brand was not the only rider to struggle with her equipment, as race winner Schreiber and third-placed finisher Manon Bakker were both forced to change bikes due to frozen pedals.

Despite having technical issues of her own, Bakker was hoping for more snow as the cyclo-cross World Cup continues in Tabor on Sunday.

“I made too many mistakes to really get into the win. I think everybody struggled with their pedals, I couldn’t clip in at all. I had a mechanical with my first bike and had to change, which is where I lost quite a lot of time," Bakker said.

“I came back, but that was it. I'd rather hope for more snow (at Tabor on Sunday). I think I'm the only one who was really smiling at the weather.”

It was Brand’s first outing in these snow conditions after missing previous World Cup rounds in Val di Sole.

“We haven’t had too often the chance for it,” said Brand on the snow conditions before the opening World Cup round. “I missed the World Cups in Val di Sole. This is something different again as there is not as much snow everywhere [on the course itself].”

Brand won the overall cyclo-cross World Cup series last year after sweeping the opening seven rounds in a commanding season.

However, this season the Dutch woman has found racing much closer and was beaten on two occasions last weekend by Sara Casasola. In the second of those races, Brand fell heavily at the X2O 'cross in Beringen and commented about suffering rib pain afterwards.

"My rib hurts a little. I now have to breathe well and calmly," Brand said. “It needs to heal again. It remains to be seen how this will develop in the coming days. You can do nothing but wait and let it recover.”

Brand won the World Cup overall by 97 points ahead of Aniek Van Alphen (777TV CX Team). However, with Van Alphen finishing runner-up in Ostrava, the pressure is on the two-time World Champion as they head to the second round in Tabor on Sunday.

items.title: World Cup Ostrava: Thibau Nys surges ahead of Tibor Del Grosso to triumph in elite men's snowy first round
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Reigning European champion Thibau Nys (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions) held off Dutch champion Tibor Del Grosso (Alpecin-Premier Tech) on the final corner and won the opening round of the UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava, Czech Republic.

Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw Cycling Team) then nabbed the final spot on the podium with a final push through blowing snow ahead of of Cameron Mason (777tv CX Team) in fourth and Jente Michels (Alpecin-Premier Tech) in fifth.

Nys continued his string of victories, dominating the X2O Trofee series with a trio of wins this month and taking the ’cross continental title.

"It was a really difficult one, but I think it's in my top three of most beautiful cyclo-cross victories. I think the fans, the atmosphere, the chorus, the snow makes it one to remember," Nys told broadcasters at the finish.

Nys let out a loud scream as he crossed the line, only able to drop Del Grosso in the final 200 metres with a more powerful sprint. Nys admitted he overcame two slow leaks and pitted for a fresh bike twice, then used "good technique" to seal the victory.

"I had two flat tyres, so it kept pushing me a little bit back. I didn't lose a lot because it [tyre pressure] was slowly going out, but it kept pushing me a bit out of the race. And then when I found my way to the front, I tried to make a move and push hard. Then on the last lap, I managed it perfectly and did a good sprint," he noted.

"I was feeling way, way better than the last two weekends, just physically. But then of course you come here on a circuit where it's difficult to release the full power, so the fact that I can finish it off like this is a proof that my cyclo-cross skills are still there."

The World Cup season opened with two rounds in Czechia, the elite fields competing Friday in Ostrava in the only night races of the 12-round series. Floodlights illuminated a blanket of snow covering the venue, with the temperature holding steady for most of the afternoon at -1°C, but the wind chill making it feel five degrees colder.

Niels Vandeputte (Alpecin-Premier Tech Development) put on the power beside Nys from the start and took the front spot on the twisty course. Vanthourenhout and Del Grosso then led the long line of riders through the first pass of the finish line, riding in 6:36, which was the slowest lap of the nine.

There were narrow ruts instead of mud from the elite women’s race as the temperatures remained below freezing, and holiday lights sprinkled around the circuit. Amid the sounds of cowbells and cheers, the ringing of disc brakes was heard with constant speed changes as the track was slippery.

On the start of lap three, Gerben Kuypers (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) took the lead ahead of Del Grosso and Pauwels teammate Vanthourenhout as small gaps began to form in the field of 75 riders.

At the mid-point of the contest, 10 riders settled in at the front - Del Grosso between the Pauwels Sauzen duo of Kuypers and Nieuwenhuis, then Vanthourenhout, Nys, Kuypers, Jent Michels, Yordi Corsus, Witse Meeussen, Felipe Orts and Cameron Mason.

It was Nys who drove the pace at the front to start the sixth and seventh laps, the second time carving a gap of five seconds to chasers across the stairs. However, he had to slow to bang one foot on the pedal to clear debris from his cleat and it was game-on again. Dutch ’cross champion Del Grosso, Vanthourenhout, Kuypers, Michels and Mason made it to his back wheel, but others were distanced for good.

On the final lap, Del Grosso took command at the front with Nys glued to his wheel, Vanthourenhout third and Mason in fourth. In a corner, Vanthourenhout dove to the front of the lead trio and held the position into the tricky descent from the stairs, while Nys made a pass of Del Grosso to nab second position.

With the wind blowing light snow, Del Grosso and Nys went back into the front positions, Vanthourenhout losing momentum in a corner before the barriers. Nys made the pass before the short steps feature and drove the sprint to the line and keep his winning streak alive.

items.title: 'Bring great bike racing to the people' - Two events debut at USA CRITS for seven races compressed across 22 days in 2027
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The Tour of Newport News Criterium and Charlotte Criterium make debuts in the USA CRITS series in 2027, with the compact collection of seven one-day races now spanning 22 days for overall elite rider and team titles, condensing the calendar by a full month.

In its 18th season, with races clustered in four states of the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast regions, the series opener will take place in Newport News, Virginia, on April 10. The finale is set for the High Line Criterium in Suwanee, Georgia, on May 1.

Noticeably absent from the calendar is the Sunny King Criterium, which had been the lead-off event the past three seasons. Anniston has hosted races for state age-group championships as well as collegiate conference championships and organisers will continue to hold two days of racing for a 25th edition April 10-11.

“Nearly 20 years after launching the series, we're still bringing the best riders in the country to communities that embrace the excitement of professional cycling," Gene Dixon, founder of Athens Twilight Criterium and owner of Swagger LLC that produces USA CRITS, said in a press release.

"When we started Athens Twilight in 1980, the idea was simple: bring great bike racing to the people. USA CRITS was built on that same philosophy."

Dixon told that the compact calendar helped simplify travel for riders and teams, especially those traveling from outside the US. While the final set of three races continue to conflict for some teams with Tour of the Gila, April 28-May 2, the earlier finish for the criterium series opens travel for all teams to compete at Tour de Bloom, May 12-16. Also a postivite is that the USA CRITS calendar does not bump into rushed travel to Washington, D.C. for the Amazon Armed Forces Cycling Classic, now early June.

All USA CRITS races will provide live streaming, produced by Swagger. Last year's prize purse totalled $200,000, with equal payouts for elite men and women across individual races and overall series classifications. The USA CRITS D1 Team programme also returns in 2027, with eligible teams provided travel stipends.

The Tour of Newport News is a three-day, five-race event that takes place on the Virginia Peninsula, on the banks of the Hampton Roads harbor near the Atlantic Ocean. USA Cycling-sanctioned events that comprise the omnium include a points race at Todd Stadium, a hill climb up an eight-story parking garage, a time trial and two criteriums. Only the Newport News Twilight Criterium, under the street lights on Saturday night, will set the standings for USA CRITS on Saturday, April 10.

The Charlotte Criterium is a new race that takes place on Friday, April 23, the night before the Winston Salem Cycling Classic. Specifics about the location of the course and start times will be confirmed in the coming months.

A rearview radar has become a must-have accessory for many road cyclists, alerting them to approaching vehicles, how close they are and how fast they're going.

One of the best available is the Garmin RLT515, and this Black Friday it's got 25% off at Backcountry, dropping the price from $200 to just $149.99 for US buyers.

In the UK, Sigma Sports has the RTL515 discounted to £117, down from £169.99; that's a hefty 31% saving.

The market for rearview radars is now quite crowded, but it was Garmin that introduced the category with its first-generation Varia, and it's still arguably the leading brand.

The RTL515 has a claimed detection distance of 140m, although on a straight road in good conditions we reckon it's significantly greater than this. The 220-degree detection angle ensures that vehicles approaching from side roads are detected as well.

The radar links up to a cycling computer, a smartwatch or a phone via Bluetooth or ANT+ and alerts you when a vehicle is detected. It's device-agnostic, so it will work with any brand of cycling computer, not just Garmin.

A fast-approaching vehicle generates a different alert from a slower-moving one, and cycling computers and other devices display how close it is. Once it's passed, there's an all-clear alert.

Four lighting modes include a day flash with 16 hours of claimed battery runtime, a night flash, a constant mode and Peloton mode that lowers the output so that other riders behind you in a group aren't dazzled.

The RTL515 is low in weight at a claimed 71g and is supplied with a robust mount, O-rings to secure it to your seatpost and spacers to suit different seatpost shapes.

REI has a similar 25% Black Friday discount on the Garmin Varia RCT715, which includes a camera in addition to the tail light and is priced down from $400 to $299.99, while the newer Varia RearVue 820 is priced down from $300 to $249.99.

items.title: Mini-pumps begone! The Cycplus AS2 electric inflator is a third off this Black Friday, making it cheaper than many hand pumps

It's supplied with a hose, which you can use to reduce the risk of melting the valve on a TPU inner tube, although it can be directly hooked up to your valve if you're running tubeless or have a less delicate tube to inflate.

We've spent too many hours standing by the road pumping up tubes not to be impressed by the Cycplus pump's around a minute to inflate a tyre to 50psi and it should manage two tyres on a charge.

It's had a battery upgrade since launch too, upping the capacity from 300mAh to 400mAh, which Cycplus reckons will get two 25mm tyres to 110psi, if you like a firm ride. An LED indicator changes from green to amber to red as charge drops.

Plug it into a USB-C charger and it will recharge in a claimed time of just 25 minutes. It comes with the necessary USB-C cable, a range of adapters and a silicone protective sleeve, plus a water resistant ziplock pouch.

If you want to check that your tyre is really up to 110psi before setting off, the Cycplus AS2 Pro has a digital pressure gauge built in. It's a little larger and heavier, but will still fit in a jersey pocket with space to space.

items.title: World Cup Ostrava: Marie Schreiber cruises to first round elite women's victory on snow-packed course in Czech Republic
items.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
items.content:
After the disappointment of being relegated at the European Championships, Marie Schreiber (SD Worx-Protime) bounced back with a triumph at the first UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup of the season in Ostrava, Czech Republic.

The Luxembourg rider took a solo win in snowy conditions, ahead of runner-up Aniek van Alphen (777 CX Team) and third-placed Manon Bakker. Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon-SRAM) took fourth, while Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado (Fenix-Premier Tech) was forced to settle for fifth after a crash with two laps to go.

After a slow start and what appeared to be pedal issues, world champion Lucinda Brand (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureu Lions) finished 15th at 2:25 behind the day’s winner and new World Cup leader, Schreiber.

“This was special. It was really nice and something completely new. Yeah, I’ve done one snowy race before but it was a new course, an evening race, it was snowy and cold, and the crowds were amazing, so it was really special. It was awesome,” Schreiber said in a post-race interview to broadcasters.

“At the first part, I had some problems with me pedals, like everyone did, it was really hard to clip in, but then I changed bikes and it was better. Like last week, I needed 20 minutes to get into the race ... but I just settled into a rhythm and try not to make mistakes.

"I couldn’t go all out but had to go with the flow and be really smooth. I managed well, and once I caught Aniek, I could see on some parts I was stronger, I played it smart on the last lap and luckily it worked out.”

The cyclo-cross stars lined up for the opening round of the UCI World Cup under snowy conditions, facing deep ruts along the circuit in Ostrava.

Although Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) was missing from the start, the field was stacked with the likes of world champion Brand, Sara Casasola (Crelan-Corendon) and Fem van Empel (Specialized TMRW), all among the favourites for the night-time cyclo-cross race.

Also on the start line was Shirin van Anrooij, who will have to start the races in a neutral kit for the first five weeks of the cyclo-cross season under UCI regulations, until January 1, when she can wear the kit of her new team, Canyon-SRAM.

A slow start for Brand and Casasola saw the pair racing much further back on the opening circuit than expected, as van Alphen immediately took the lead.

After the first lap, Van Alphen was followed by Alvarado and Schreiber in her wake. She continued her dominance, distancing her rivals and holding an eight-second advantage on the fourth of seven laps ahead of a chasing Schreiber and Bakker. Further back, Alvarado was 22 seconds back, and Kristýna Zemanova (Crelan-Corendon) was 42 seconds.

Although Brand appeared to be gaining time back, moving up to sixth place about 25 seconds back, bad luck struck, and she was forced into the pits for a bike change after a problem with her pedals. She lost significant time, chasing in 22nd place at 1:34 behind the leader.

Bad luck for Alvarado, too, who crashed on the fifth of seven laps, over the handlebars, through the deep snowy ruts, but was up and back on her bike quickly, chasing in fourth place, but with Backstedt close behind.

Under two laps to go, Van Alphen still held a small lead, but with only one second ahead of Schreiber, the pair reconnected as they hit the snow circuit, resetting the race for the victory. The race became even more interesting as Bakker caught the leading duo after a new fastest lap of 7:04, showing strong late-race form.

Schreiber made the winning move on the last lap, opening a small gap to Bakker and Van Alphen, who appeared to struggle to clip in to her pedals.

They were no match for Schreiber, who crossed the line for the win, with Van Alphen taking second and Bakker third, not only winning the first round but also taking the series lead.

items.title: Netcompany Ineos cancel new transfer Harold Tejada before 2027 season amid biological passport anti-doping investigation
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Netcompany Ineos have agreed to terminate the agreement with one of their new signings for the 2027 season before his contract even begins on January 1, amid a provisional suspension and investigation into the biological passport of Colombian rider Harold Tejada.

Not even 50 days have passed since Ineos announced Tejada as a new name set to bolster their climbing ranks, but after he revealed on Friday afternoon that he had been notified by the International Testing Agency (ITA) of an anti-doping disciplinary proceeding against him, an announcement from the British team followed an hour later.

"Netcompany INEOS and Harold Tejada have agreed to end their agreement for the 2027 season, before he was due to join the team on 1 January," read a post from the team on X.

A winner of a Paris-Nice stage this season, Tejada was set to be one of nine new transfers already announced for Netcompany Ineos in 2027, as they look to rebuild back to their former GC glory.

Tejada maintains his innocence. His statement highlighted that the suspension is "a temporary measure, which does not constitute a sanction nor a definitive decision", and he confirmed that he will be working with a legal and medical team to "exercise my defense before the relevant bodies, through the established channels."

The ITA released a press release, echoing Tejada's statement, but also confirming that it had charged Tejada with an anti-doping rule violation (ADRV) "for the use of a prohibited substance or a prohibited method based on unexplained abnormalities in his athlete biological passport (ABP)."

"The ITA reports that the ABP¹ of Colombian road cyclist Harold Alfonso Tejada Canacue has returned an Adverse Passport Finding (APF)² due to unexplained abnormalities in the values of his haematological ABP," read the release.

"Specifically, a panel of experts has confirmed that the rider has a case to answer, as, after reviewing the rider’s explanation, the panel maintained that the abnormalities in his ABP are highly likely to have been caused by the administration of a prohibited substance and/or a prohibited method.

"The rider has been informed of the charge and has the right to provide additional information.  The rider has the possibility to accept the consequences for his violation or to request for the matter to be referred to the UCI Anti-Doping Tribunal for a hearing.

"Further, in accordance with the UCI anti-doping rules and article 6.2.1 of the UCI regulations for results management (UCI RMR), a mandatory provisional suspension has been imposed on the rider. The rider has the right to challenge the provisional suspension and ask for its lifting."

As listed on the ITA's website: "The ABP is an individual electronic profile that monitors selected biological variables of an athlete. It contains the results of the athletes’ urine and blood samples, which are tracked consistently. Any significant variation from normal levels can be assessed for possible manipulation. At the ITA, ABP management is performed by a specialist unit of experts who liaise with the Athlete Passport Management Units (APMUs) and ABP Expert Panels in order to issue further targeted testing or in case of adverse or atypical findings."

Tejada's statement in full

"To the general public, cycling fans, and everyone who has accompanied me throughout my career: on November 26, 2026, I was notified by the International Testing Agency (ITA), on behalf of the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), of the initiation of an anti-doping disciplinary proceeding against me.

"While this proceeding is being resolved, I am provisionally suspended in relation to an investigation into my biological passport.

"I want to clarify that this suspension is a temporary measure, which does not constitute a sanction or a final decision.

"From day one, I have acted with diligence and responsibility, providing all requested information in a timely manner. I will continue to do so throughout the entire process, with full respect for the anti-doping authorities and cycling institutions.

"My legal and medical team will work to exercise my defense before the relevant bodies, through the established channels.

"In consideration of the confidentiality of the proceeding, I will refrain from making additional statements while the case is ongoing.

"I deeply thank my family, my friends, and all the people who have expressed their support to me during these days. I ask you, with all due respect, to understand this moment and respect our privacy.

"Harold Alfonso Tejada Canacue"

The Castelli Perfetto is a familiar name in winter cycling. Alongside the iconic Gabba, it has been a go-to piece of kit for riders for more than a decade.

When Castelli updated its Perfetto jacket in September, it took customer feedback on board. Riders had told the brand they wanted more warmth than the previous version offered - something our Associate Editor Josh Croxton also highlighted in his review of the Perfetto RoS 3. The new Perfetto 4 aims to address that feedback, with added warmth for cooler rides.

Despite only launching around two months ago, the latest Perfetto is already discounted, with deals available across a range of sizes and colourways, and in both the men's and women's ranges.

As for fit, Castelli describes the Perfetto 4 as having a race-inspired cut. Previous versions have impressed us with their fit, offering a close fit without being overly restrictive, while still leaving enough room underneath for an extra layer if needed.

items.title: Mark Cavendish’s former coach joins Ben Swift among the staff reinforcements at Netcompany Ineos
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
British WorldTour team Netcompany Ineos have announced three new additions to their support staff, with the recently-retired Ben Swift, Vasilis Anastopoulos and Professor Asker Jeukendrup joining in the team’s backroom.

As expected, after a 19-year career as a rider which included 15 race victories and two podium finishes in Milan-Sanremo, Swift will take up a role as one of the team’s sports directors. Having switched from a sprinter and Classics rider to a role as a road captain in recent years, he should be able to develop those leadership skills in his new role.

"I know how much the people around a rider matter, because I've been that rider," Swift said in a team press release. "I'll miss racing, no doubt. But I'm excited to give something back from the car, keep learning, and bring the same commitment I had as a rider."

Anastopoulos, also a former professional rider, is perhaps best known as the coach who oversaw Mark Cavendish’s return to winning form during the sprinter’s second spell with Soudal-QuickStep. He then went with Cavendish when he moved to the Astana team, and guided the sprinter to his 35th and record-breaking Tour de France stage win.

He joins Netcompany from the Kazakh team, where he’s been head of performance since 2023, and will join the team’s coaching staff in a "senior role".

Finally, Prof. Jeukendrup joins the team as director of physiology and nutrition after a career working in high performance sport, including across multiple sports as performance manager with the Dutch TeamNL and two years as director of sport strategy at Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, a role he left last month.

It’s been a busy week for Netcompany Ineos, who first announced that former Tour de France and Giro d’Italia winner Egan Bernal extended his contract, apparently until the end of 2029. Then, hours after that announcement, they revealed seven other current riders were staying with the British outfit, with Connor Swift, Ben Swift’s cousin, committing until the end of the 2029 season as well.

items.title: Cobbled Classics reveal revamped routes as E3 Saxo Classic and Dwars door Vlaanderen make changes for 2027
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The pair are among the most important races of the March-April Classics block, both falling in the week before the Tour of Flanders along with In Flanders Fields, as well as being WorldTour and Women's WorldTour races in their own right.

On Thursday, organisers of the E3 Saxo Classic presented their race's new look for its 70th edition on March 26, 2027.

The race will be slightly shortened from 208.8km to 207.8km, while the number of climbs in the race has also been reduced, with 14 climbs featuring rather than 16. Organisers enacted the latter change after requests from riders and teams.

"We received a request from the peloton to adjust the course in terms of elevation gain. Our E3 DNA remains the same. It remains an attractive course. We still seek out cobblestone sections and steep climbs. That remains identical," Seppe Seynhaeve of the race organisation told .

For the most part, the route of the E3 Saxo Classic – which starts and ends in Harelbeke – will be the same as the 2026 edition, with the brutal hill zone in the second half retaining the two ascents of the Oude Kwaremont as well as the Taaienberg, Eikenberg, Paterberg, and Tiegemberg, among others.

The two climbs cut from the route will be the Berg Ten Stene and Oude Kruisberg, which lay after 85km and 108km in the 2026 race. 14 named climbs – among many other smaller ones – and nine cobbled sectors remain on the route.

In contrast to the E3 Saxo Classic, the next edition of Dwars door Vlaanderen will be tougher than the last.

The 81st edition of the men's race, which falls on March 31 next year, will feature 16 climbs, up from 12 in the 2026 edition. The Kluisberg climb is in for the Volkegemberg, while the trio of the Berg Ten Houte, Knokteberg-Trieu, and Hotond will each be tackled three times rather than twice, as was the case in 2026.

Two loops of those three climbs will come in the middle of the race, while the final 72km remain unchanged. The race will run for 185km from Roeselare to Waregem.

"We have strengthened our DNA. We are adding the Kluisberg, which replaces the Volkegemberg, and we will cross the Trieu three times," Pavel Desmet, chairman of the KSV Waregem Vooruit, told .

The women's race, meanwhile, will be run for the 15th time next spring with a 130km route starting and ending in Waregem.

A more challenging route awaits the women's peloton, too, with 11 climbs on the menu, up from eight climbs this year. The race will feature a new loop of the Knokteberg-Trieu, Hotond, and Mariaborrestraat, while the final 72km will be identical to the men's Dwars door Vlaanderen.

"The riders will be presented with 130km featuring eleven climbs and six cobblestone sections along the way. Just like with the men, the Hellestraat – Kluisberg duo forms the gateway to the Flemish Ardennes." Desmet said of the women's race.

items.title: Tadej Pogačar’s neo-pro salary revealed, as his agent details big rise in wages for young talents
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Tadej Pogačar's agent Alex Carera has revealed how the market for young riders has completely changed since the Slovenian turned pro back in 2019, with wages now eclipsing those Pogačar received.

Speaking to , Carera said Pogačar's first professional contract, having won the Tour de l'Avenir and Giro della Regione Friuli-Venezia Giulia in 2018, saw him net a €60,000 pro contract.

Now, eight years later, things are completely different, he said.

"Tadej's first professional contract involved an annual salary of €60,000, plus a bonus of €20,000 if he won the Tour de l'Avenir that year," Carera, co-head of the A&J Sports agency, told .

"All young riders in those years signed their first professional contract for €70-90,000. Certainly not for more money."

Today, riders in a similar position, such as those who have won the Tour de l'Avenir, stand to earn a lot more when they ascend to the WorldTour shortly afterwards.

Joseph Blackmore, Paul Seixas and Lorenzo Finn stand among the recent winners of the French race, while Jarno Widar, Jakob Omrzel and Finn have won the past three editions of the Giro d'Italia Next Gen. All have top-level contracts heading into 2027.

"If you win the Tour de l'Avenir now, you sign for €300,000," Carera said.

Budgets and wages have risen across the board since Pogačar turned pro, with median WorldTour team budgets rising from approximately €18 million to around €28 million between 2019 and 2025. In 2026, total team budgets topped €663 million, up by €33 million from 2025.

As for Pogačar, it goes without saying that his pay has exploded given his on-bike success since that initial €60,000 contract. He now takes home a reported €8 million per year as the highest-paid rider in cycling.

items.title: 'He's not a guy that just mails it in... he's always been a real killer in races' – Why George Bennett is backing Primož Roglič for 'special results' as former teammates reunite at NSN
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
When Primož Roglič was presented the option of NSN Cycling Team as an option to extend his career into 2027, who else was he going to call other than a former teammate of six seasons, George Bennett?

Just six months apart in age, the New Zealand national champion raced as a GC domestique alongside Roglič for what was then LottoNL-Jumbo and then Jumbo-Visma. During those years together, Bennett was part of the winning team from Roglič's first of five Grand Tour triumphs at the 2019 Vuelta a España, but also took in the ultimate low of losing the 2020 Tour de France to Tadej Pogačar on the penultimate day, only for it to be followed by the ultimate bounce back at the subsequent Vuelta, where his new teammate claimed the second of his four red jerseys.

Few riders have experienced the resilience of Roglič – which has made him so successful but also so compelling throughout his years in the peloton – first-hand like Bennet has, and the Kiwi isn't expecting him to slow down now that he's at NSN at 37.

"Well, I knew because he called me, and it was a very quick turnaround. We had a quick chat about the team and basically asked me to give him some pros and cons, and then within a couple of days it was announced, and it all went really fast," Bennett told on Wednesday when asked about how he experienced the surprise late transfer announcement.

"Was I surprised? No, I mean, I guess I was surprised it happened so late in the piece. But early on, I thought that he would be a really good signing. I knew he was up and knew that Red Bull was not going to be a viable place for him to stay.

"And I'd mentioned to them ages ago that he's not a guy that just mails it in and goes out for a contract; he's always been a real killer in races, and I don't really think he's slowing down.

"He's not personally getting slower. It's just that there's been this revolution, and the rate of improvement of other guys has been exponential. And you have these young guys coming through at a crazy level, but I think actually this year there were times he was better than ever, and it just didn't line up that he got to show that in races.

"Hit by a car before the Vuelta, and obviously team priorities at Red Bull, and there's a lot of things like that going on, so I think here in this environment with a team around him and everyone backing him, I think we'll still see a lot of pretty special results."

Looking back on some of those Grand Tour victories as teammates from seven and six years ago, Bennett compared the jeopardy and occasional drama which has followed Roglič with that of another of his former teammates, and the Slovenian's compatriot, Pogačar.

Roglič's incredibly successful career is one that has been marked by crashes and hardship, all of which he has come out the other side of to still be hitting out as one of the top riders in the world.

Even this most recent season – one which almost saw him head into retirement before figuring out that he did want to continue and finding a place at NSN – was one where getting knocked off his bike by a driver almost derailed his main goal of racing the Vuelta, where he eventually finished an impressive second on the comeback from injury.

"I think starting late, there's always a sense that it could go wrong as well," said Bennett, referring to Roglič's move across from ski jumping to road cycling. "There are these dramatic moments of just crashes and last-minute losses, but for me, what was so special early on is having a guy that could just – if you could get him close – he had this unbelievable finish on him.

"I think he can fight like not many guys can, and can fight all the time, you know. Losing the Tour that year [in 2020], we got up and we won the Vuelta, and did it again the next year.

"I think he appreciates the opportunity he has, and you know he'll just go to the end, especially if you do a job, and that's all you can ask as a helper. But there has always been a sense of sort of drama around him because as much as of the things that go right, there's also some of the things that go wrong – whereas someone like Tadej doesn't miss. Tadej is just knocking out win, win, win, win. There's less jeopardy in a way unless you're talking Roubaix or something; it's more of a guarantee."

It's a kind of jeopardy that has made the flame burn even stronger for Bennett when it comes to motivation, wanting to ride to more successes with Roglič as they reunite as teammates.

"I think for me, having been with him for so long and being part of those losses, it kind of has given me a bit of a soft spot for him, that you know I want to step up again and try and remedy a few of the losses and try and get back those highs," he said.

A new era of GC racing for NSN

Bennett is relishing the opportunity to race as a domestique deluxe for any of the new leaders into 2027, enjoying the team's shift after several recent years of operating as a mountain breakaway hunter.

"Oh, I love it. I mean, on a personal level, that's what I would say my expertise is: being a GC domestic. Being in bike races, I'm realistic now; I'm not winning these mountaintops anymore," said Bennet over a video call on Wednesday.

"But it's still what I love doing, so to be part of a team with that in mind, it's a different mindset, and you have to be a bit more clinical. You have to know when to push, when not to push; there are so many aspects of riding GC, and it's not just climbing domestiques that we need; it's also the guys on the flat for staying out of trouble, and the whole approach has to change. It's less opportunistic, more methodical, and more like turning over every stone, and that trickles down to the whole team.

"For me personally, it's what I love doing, and I think that's when I've been at my best as being a helper for these GC guys, and we've got Primož, but we've also got Richie, Buitrago, and Van Eetvelt, so I think I'm staring down the barrel of what's potentially a very busy year, but at the same time, it's very exciting."

As a team who ranked 19th in the world last season with only 16 wins to their name, Bennett described how NSN have been able to celebrate big when things have paid off, but with a much-improved roster in 2027, those occasions may well become much more frequent.

"I think for NSN the highs go really far – we haven't won a lot of races, and we weren't necessarily one of these huge teams, but now we kind of are, and some of the races I've won on this team with [Ethan] Vernon, with Brady [Gilmore], with Stevie [Williams], they feel like unbelievable because, like, holy shit, we won, and I think that's that's special," he said.

"Now we have those same guys, but we also have some big champions to go with it."

items.title: Rabobank returns to title sponsorship as new naming sponsor of Visma-Lease a Bike Women
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike have unveiled a new title sponsor for their women's team, with Rabobank making its return to a title sponsorship role after a 10-year absence.

The team will officially be known as Rabobank-Lease a Bike Women’s Pro Cycling Team from 2027

The Dutch bank, which pulled out of men's cycling at the end of 2012 – after a long sponsorship of this very team – and out of women's cycling at the end of 2026, has been investing again in the sport in recent years, but Friday's announcement marks a significant step back towards its prominence of old.

Friday's announcement of Rabobank's sponsorship exclusively concerned Visma-Lease a Bike's women's team, so as it stands, a new title sponsor for the men's team is still unknown.

That means that the two squads will have different names for the first time, having shared names since the women's team launched in 2021.

"Given our shared history, the return of the Rabobank name as a title partner is a special moment," said Visma-Lease a Bike CEO Richard Plugge.

"It demonstrates Rabobank’s confidence in our team and in the future of women’s cycling. We are proud to build on that confidence together."

Remarkably, the team’s two star riders will be pulling on Rabobank-emblazoned jerseys once more, with both Marianne Vos and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot having ridden for the former Rabobank-sponsored women’s team (a separate team to the men’s) during the bank’s five sponsorship years from 2012 to 2016.

Rabobank’s tumultuous relationship with pro cycling

Rabobank’s association with cycling stretches back to 1996, when it began its long-running title sponsorship of the men’s team that is now known as Visma-Lease a Bike. The team was one of the most prominent forces in the men’s peloton throughout the quarter of a century that Rabobank sponsored the team, and it is again now, but there was a fallow period when the Dutch bank withdrew at the end of 2012.

The US Anti-Doping Agency’s landmark 2012 report into doping by Lance Armstrong and others had recently been published, and Rabobank publicly stated it had lost faith that men’s cycling could be a clean sport, though it did continue its title sponsorship of the women’s team for another four seasons.

And they were highly successful seasons, with Vos enjoying the most prolific years of her extraordinary career as a Rabobank rider. She and Ferrand-Prévot kept the elite women’s road race rainbow jersey within the team for three years – Vos winning back-to-back world titles in 2012 and 2013, followed by Ferrand-Prévot in 2014. It was a similar story in cyclo-cross, with Vos winning the world title in 2012, 2013, and 2014, and Ferrand-Prévot winning it in 2015.

Rabobank withdrew its sponsorship at the end of 2016, at which point Ferrand-Prévot moved to Canyon-SRAM, while Vos stayed as the team became WM3, Waowdeals, and CCC-Liv, leaving three years before it merged with the current LIV-AlUla-Jayco team to join this current team on its 2021 launch as Jumbo-Visma Women.

Rabobank faded from view, but in recent years it has shown a willingness to return to cycling, and to pro cycling. In 2025, it returned to the Visma-Lease a Bike team as a minor sponsor, and its logo has adorned the jersey of the men’s and women’s squads since July of last year. It was recently announced that Rabobank will be the title sponsor of the NXT Classic race.

On top of that, since last year it has been the title sponsor of the Rabo Dikke Banden Races, which are youth participation events in the Netherlands.

"When we returned to cycling last year, our ambition was to give the sport a boost, with a focus on elite sport, talent development and grassroots sport in the Netherlands," said Rabobank board member Carlo van Kemenade.

"Our return generated a great deal of positivity and enthusiasm. By taking on a greater role in women’s cycling, we are building on that momentum. This reflects who we are as a cooperative bank and our commitment to local communities.

"From the first introduction to the sport to competing at the highest level, we want to contribute to a sport in which talent has even more opportunities to flourish. For us, that is the power of investing in sport together."

items.title: Is this cycling’s ‘Moneyball’ moment? Inside the arms race for UCI points
items.author: James Witts
items.content:
"After my presentation in Barcelona, teams wanted to chat and compare their models with mine. This is a growing field, whether it's in search of points or simply improving performance as a whole." That's Louis Van Gaelen. The Belgian's undertaking a PhD in health and artificial intelligence at the University of Antwerp. As a side project, the keen cyclist dug deep into professional cycling and, as his presentation at this year's Science & Cycling Conference revealed, 'roster optimisation for maximal UCI points'. It's not the sexiest of titles, but Van Gaelen's hobby, aligned with the work of an increasing number of data scientists around the sport, is proving critical for not only a team's success but their survival. It's time to talk about the merits of not aiming for victory…

How does the system work?

The current UCI promotion and relegation system, rolled out in 2020, works in three-year cycles with 18 licences available to the men's WorldTour. The Women's WorldTour has 15 licences; however, demand for these spots is less competitive due to the limited number of teams willing to make the step up.

The 2026 season was the first season in the latest cycle, meaning points earned up to the end of 2028 will determine the WorldTour line-up for 2029 to 2031.

"All points from UCI-sanctioned races count towards the team total, but only the points accrued from the top-20 scoring riders," Van Gaelen adds. "Remaining at WorldTour can make or break a team."

That's because WorldTour status guarantees teams entry into cycling's biggest races, including the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España. Relegation means losing automatic invitations, reducing television exposure, sponsor value and commercial income. It also makes attracting top riders harder, potentially creating a vicious circle of declining competitiveness.

The UCI also assesses a team's non-sporting side, including the financial stability of the team, which is why they granted Team Picnic PostNL a truncated 12-month licence for 2026. At the time of the ruling, the Dutch team hadn't finalised medium- to long-term backing with one of its sponsors, leaving the required fiscal guarantees for 2027 and 2028 incomplete. The Picnic turbulence continues to this day, heightened by serious allegations about team culture, with December 8, 2026 a key date in the calendar, as that's when the UCI is expected to confirm 2027 registrations.

But let's return to sporting criteria, as that's why the likes of Van Gaelen are in demand. His work looked to answer which riders a team should sign; which races each rider should participate in; and how a team can maximise its total UCI points across a season. The search involved combining two technologies: machine learning and mathematical optimisation.

Machine learning utilised 10 seasons' worth of data, covering thousands of riders and their previous performances, in addition to race profiles and course difficulty. "Inputting the course profiles was a laborious job," Van Gaelen says. "It involved uploading many, many course GPX files from an internet forum." Van Gaelen's machine-learning model then predicted the likely finishing order of riders in individual races, which were translated into expected UCI points using the relevant race's points scale.

The second part, mathematical optimisation, aimed to build the perfect roster by, for instance, matching climbers and sprinters to races where they're likeliest to score, by reducing clashes between teammates and setting a race-day ceiling at 85 days.

"With our optimised roster and focusing on one team in particular, we increased the points per rider from an average of 375.3 to 824.7," Van Gaelen explains. "Of course, there are limitations – our model didn't take into account fatigue, for example – but it's a promising proof of concept."

If Van Gaelen's work is good on paper, XDS Astana's is good in practice. The Kazakh team are the poster boys for optimising rosters in search of UCI points. At the end of the 2024 season, they were facing almost certain relegation, languishing 21st in the annual UCI rankings. But that's when they made one of their most important signings of recent times: data scientist Morgan Saussine.

One of the key implementations from Saussine's work was to prioritise top-10 finishes over individual victories. While historically teams would often organise their racing around one protected leader, with teammates sacrificing their own results to help that rider win, Saussine, who was unavailable for interview at the time of writing, identified there was much lower-hanging fruit to pick from in search of points.

Astana set about assembling a squad capable of scoring across different race categories, terrains and stages of the season. Into the squad came 14 new faces, including experienced riders such as Wout Poels, Diego Ulissi, Fausto Masnada and Mike Teunissen. The arrival of Chinese sponsor XDS provided additional financial resources to support the change. It worked, as they shot up the rankings to finish fourth in 2025 and so preserve their WorldTour status. Cofidis went down.

"Given the situation XDS Astana faced at the beginning of the 2025 season, when the team urgently needed UCI points, it's easy to see why a rider like Christian Scaroni was so invaluable," says researcher Simon Lucat. "Here's a rider who regularly finishes in the top-10 across a demanding race calendar."

Scaroni's importance to the cause was also highlighted this season with the 29-year-old Italian finishing inside the top-10 of one-day races or stages 33 times. He also won the overall at the Tour of Oman.

Lucat, a lifelong cycling fan and an economics student at Bocconi University in Milan, Italy, researched the inherent paradox that is professional cycling: results are attributed to individual riders, but they're collectively produced by a team.

"One of the main findings of my research is that the combined quality of the riders surrounding the leader can be just as important as the quality of the leader himself when it comes to accumulating UCI points," he says. "Strong teammates are valuable not only because they can help the leader achieve a better result, but also because they can score points themselves."

"The balance may also depend on the type of race," he adds. "Paris-Roubaix, for example, stood out in my analysis as a race where squad depth appeared to be particularly important. This makes sense if you think about the nature of the race, where a puncture or a crash can completely change a team's plans. Having several competitive riders gives you more options."

The original points detective

The likes of Van Gaelen and Lucat are building on the foundations laid by Raul Banqueri. In 2020, the diligent Spaniard waded through the UCI's 400-page road-racing regulations PDF in search of content for his Twitter account. It was needle-in-a-haystack stuff, but he pricked his fingers when he unearthed what many had missed. "I saw the UCI had started using sporting criteria to award licences and distribute wildcards to the WorldTour calendar," he says, "but almost nobody was reporting on it." He did, piquing the public's interest. And that of the professionals.

"When I started publishing my analyses of the points system, a multitude of WorldTour sports directors, performance directors and cyclists started following me on Twitter," he says. "Then in 2023 I started working with the Human Powered Health women's team. That season their licence was at risk, so I prepared a dashboard with advanced statistics on results and UCI points. We thoroughly analysed the calendar to identify which races they could score the most points in with the roster they had. The team focused more on flat races and minor races, tripled their UCI points compared to 2022 (from 914 to 3354) and managed to save their WorldTour licence.

"Nowadays, UCI points are no longer as important in women's cycling, as there aren't enough teams applying for the licence, but the dashboard remains valuable for the scouting process, signings and monitoring team performance."

That year, he also collaborated on projects with Visma-Lease a Bike, assisting the team's head of strategy, Patrick Broe, while in 2025 he saddled up with the Movistar Team women's squad, helping with data and video analysis. In short, Banqueri is hot property when it comes to delivering peak points and peak performance. So, what's his assessment of sniffing out peak points performers?

"Sprinters capable of getting over hills or specialists in hilly races with high top speed are increasingly sought after to claim points," he answers. "That includes Benoît Cosnefroy, Thomas Silva, Alex Aranburu, Natnael Tesfatsion and Lukáš Kubiš, who've all scored good points for their respective teams."

"In general, one-day races are significantly more profitable than stage races," he adds. "One-day races award the same points as the general classification of a race in the same category, and stages award very few points, except in the Grand Tours. Right now, I believe that ProSeries one-day races (250 points for the winner) are the most profitable in terms of UCI points."

Banqueri says an interesting development is the strategy and recruitment adopted by ProTeams, whose goal is the top 30 of the annual ranking in search of an invite to the Grand Tours. "These teams are the ones looking the most for races outside of Europe, especially in Asia, where the level is lower, since they can score a high percentage of their total seasonal UCI points. For WorldTeams, it's less profitable to travel to race in Asia, as it causes huge fatigue for their cyclists, and the UCI points they earn don't have as much impact on their total sum of UCI points.

"Also, some of the lower-level ProTeams, like Burgos BH, have signed cyclists from more immature cycling nations to take advantage of the UCI points they can win in National Championships and Continental Championships. All Continental Championships award the same points, as do National Championships, provided the nation participated in the previous World Championships. So, being the champion of Mauritius scores the same points as being the champion of France." To that end, five of Burgos BH's eight 2025 wins came at the national championships of Mauritius, plus Uruguay, Guatemala, Mongolia and Greece. In 2026, it was three from nine wins."

In both seasons, the Spanish outfit finished comfortably in the top-30, essentially guaranteeing them a wildcard spot at the Vuelta a España. These wildcard spots are keenly fought over for the same reasons that teams strain to cling onto WorldTour status, namely media exposure and sponsor value.

Downside of chasing points

For ProTeams, this short-term points grab could have long-term consequences for the sport. "This year, Bardiani had the lowest average age (only 22.4 years, according to Pro Cycling Stats) and ultimately fell out of the top 30 in the ranking, meaning they won't be invited to the Giro d'Italia in 2027," says Banqueri. "It's a bit unfair because a team like Bardiani is essential for developing young cyclists. It means in the future they'll probably have to sign more experienced cyclists to ensure results."

If there is a future. Come the end of the 2026 season, veteran team boss Bruno Reverberi couldn't contain his anger at the points system, calling the UCI "incompetent". Reverberi told the TriCiclo podcast that with no guarantees of invitation to the world's biggest races – they'd raced every Giro d'Italia since 1982 – they could soon be out of business. "How can you spend €5 million and not have the right to race? There is no future, and cycling has no future. We've already thought about closing in two years. In fact, we have taken four or five new riders and made them sign for only one year."

The Italian team, who have nurtured the likes of Sonny Colbrelli and Giulio Pellizzari, are known for their attacking style. The UCI points system, Reverberi laments, is anti-cycling, encouraging top-10s rather than chasing glory in the breakaway. "The UCI is incompetent. They've destroyed cycling," he concluded.

He's not the only critic of chasing lesser places rather than the podium. This is from Jayco Alula's Michael Matthews earlier in 2026: "For me it's destroying cycling." And this from Serge Parsani, team manager at ProTeam Solution Tech NIPPO Rail: "It's undoubtedly an anomalous ranking."

EF Education-EasyPost boss Jonathan Vaughters went so far as to say that collecting UCI points was forcing teams to participate in too many smaller races, some of which had inadequate safety arrangements. "They're [riders] being pressured by team managers like me saying 'we've got to get points – hurry up.'"

In short, a system designed to reward sporting performance ends up discouraging teams from racing to win. It's an imperfect system. This is the result of professional cycling's imperfect business model where teams are almost wholly reliant on sponsors for survival. It's one reason why 24 teams have recently formed the Collective Cycling Group (CCG), aimed at reforming the sport and streamlining the calendar. We'll no doubt hear more of the CCG in the near future, but it does highlight the fragility of cycling at the top level. Then again, which successful organisation doesn't look to optimise resources for maximum value? Back to Lucat…

"I was also interested in the relationship between budget and team performance," he says. "You'd naturally expect wealthier teams to perform better because they can recruit stronger riders, but my findings suggest that differences in measured rider quality alone do not fully explain their advantage. A team's budget buys much more than just riders. Part of that advantage could come from better coaching, nutrition, equipment, medical support or logistics."

"Smaller teams cannot match the spending of the biggest WorldTour teams, so they have to be very smart about how they use their resources, whether in recruitment, race selection or the composition of their line-ups," Lucat continues. "This is where data analysis could be especially valuable for teams that cannot simply rely on having the strongest riders in the peloton."

In English football's top division, the three B's – Brighton and Hove Albion, Bournemouth and Brentford – are examples of sporting teams who have maximised data to punch above their collective weight. As Lucat says, if your budget is nominal, you must maximise every pound, dollar or euro. That said, one measure of success for every business is efficiency.

Just look at UAE Team Emirates-XRG. Their budget is an estimated £50 million per year – the highest in professional road cycling – but for that they've not only nurtured arguably the greatest rider of all time and dominated the rankings, they also finished third in the 2026 WorldTour budget efficiency table, put together by the website 'How to turn pro', which tracks the fiscal side of professional cycling.

Though we can't take the website's findings as gospel truth – they state that rider and team budgets are based on factors like the limited publicly available information – they do document sources, as well as featuring a public changelog and correction process.

According to the site, the UAE squad accrued 656 points per £1 million spent in 2026. That was behind second-placed XDS Astana – 749 points per million from an estimated budget of £ 23 million – and the most efficient team, Uno-X Mobility, whose 784 points per million came from an overall estimated budget of £ 16.7 million.

Keep scrolling, and you’ll upset Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his accountants, who continue to return very little on their sporting investments. Netcompany Ineos ranked 17th out of 18 in the efficiency stakes; their mooted £43.5 million resulted in just 300 points per million. Picnic were low on budget and efficiency – £16.7 million and 178 points per million – leaving them rock bottom.

Looking ahead, if Picnic survive into 2027, they have some catching up to do, finishing this season with just 2,822 points. Groupama-FDJ are the next WorldTour team, over 6,500 points ahead on 9,329, followed by NSN Cycling (9,624 points). At the ProTeam level, Tom Pidcock's Pinarello-Q36.5 team (12th in rankings) and Tudor Pro Cycling (17th) are the leading contenders for promotion.

Where does that leave us? All in all, professional cycling's points race has made data, recruitment and calendar planning essential tools of survival, not merely marginal gains. Yet when teams optimise for rankings rather than victories, the system risks distorting the sport it's meant to reward.

As Banqueri signs off, this is sport where the ultimate victory is victory itself: "Of course, teams without a large budget must seek a balance between performing in the big races, which have a greater media impact, and scoring points in minor races that give them peace of mind in the rankings. But UCI points are not the only important metric of a team's success. Movistar finished the season in 13th position but won La Vuelta. Surely Astana would have traded their season for Movistar's?"

items.title: 'When you see an opportunity, you have to act quickly' – Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand's cyclo-cross team find new sponsorship from 2027 onwards
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Sven Nys' cyclo-cross team has swiftly found a new title sponsor following the withdrawal of Glowi, owner of named sponsor Het Poetsbureau.

The team, which is led by women's world champion Lucinda Brand and men's European champion Thibau Nys, welcomes electrical retailer Elektro Loeters as a new title sponsor alongside Baloise Verzekeringen.

The new sponsorship will begin on January 1, 2027, though the length of the deal hasn't been announced.

"Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day," team manager Sven Nys said in an Instagram post announcing the news.

The deal came about quickly, the team confirmed, with Elektro Loeters only approaching them in recent weeks.

"When you see an opportunity, you have to act quickly. We immediately felt a connection with the team’s vision and ambitions. Five days later, an agreement was already on the table. It shows just how similar entrepreneurship and top-level sport are."

The team, currently known as Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions, have been the most successful during the 2026-27 cyclo-cross season so far with 12 victories.

Nys has four wins, including three rounds of the X2O Trofee, while Brand has six, including two apiece in the X2O Trofee and Superprestige. Both triumphed at the UEC Cyclo-cross European Championships in Zeddam earlier this month.

Like the team, Elektro Loeters is also experiencing success, with the company planning to open five new stores in Flanders in addition to its 10 pre-existing stores.

"Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day. Their growth story, entrepreneurial spirit and drive are a perfect match for our values. We are therefore looking forward to further developing this partnership over the coming months and putting it into action together," said Sven Nys.

Brand and Thibau Nys will lead the team in their new identity alongside other key riders Pim Ronhaar and Annemarie Worst. However, this will be Brand's penultimate cyclo-cross season, as the Dutchwoman will retire from racing in April 2028.

items.title: 'The only way for the race to grow' – Women’s Festival Elsy Jacobs race becomes part of themen'sTour of Luxembourg organisation
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Organisers of the Tour de Luxembourg men’s race will take over organisation of the women’s Festival Elsy Jacobs from 2027, has learnt.

The race, named after the first-ever women’s World Champion, began in 2008 and has taken various formats over the years, even expanding to a three-day stage race. Under the new management, it will return as a two-stage race, moving from its traditional spot in the spring to take its place on the morning of the weekend stages of the men’s Tour de Luxembourg, scheduled for September 18 and 19, 2027.

The event will remain as a 2.1, third-tier event for the time being, though the new organisation has hopes of it moving up to the Women’s ProTour level at the earliest opportunity in 2029, joining the men’s event as a second-division race.

Since its inception in 2008, Festival Elsy Jacobs has been run by SAF Zeisseng, a local cycling club from the Luxembourg City suburb of Cessanges. However, since the 2020 race was cancelled due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the race has struggled, dropping the prologue in 2023 before becoming two standalone 1.1 races the following year.

"The change is the only way for the race to grow and not to disappear," organiser Michel Zangerlé told . "The association of the Tour de Luxembourg for men will take over, with us in support. That means we are not out, but the other organisation is the leader for every financial topic."

Despite the new structure, the race will retain its name, its heritage being important to the new organisation.

"It’s not Skoda Tour de Luxembourg Femmes or something like that; it will keep the identity of Elsy Jacobs," General Secretary of the Tour de Luxembourg, Benoît Theisen, told .

"We want to give the know-how we have in the men’s race and the setup of the men's race exactly the same as for the women. And for us, it was the only way to do it was to combine it in one date because if you have it on a second date, you need the full infrastructure again.

"It’s something new; we are really excited. It will be a new start, but we don't start from zero because there's this big heritage."

The original race would always have at least one day in Jacobs’ birthplace of Garnich, and while the 2027 race start and finish locations of the stages are not yet public, it’s highly unlikely this will continue, though clearly the race’s survival is far more important.

One of the issues the original organisation faced was the haphazard way in which the women’s calendar has expanded as the sport became more professional. Its regular place at the end of April meant that, since 2023, it clashed with the Vuelta España Femenina. That meant the race was no longer able to attract the biggest teams and riders, affecting sponsorship.

While it was never a big name on the calendar, the original organisation was always a trailblazer, introducing a live stream of the action as far back as 2017, when the majority of World Tour races were not shown live.

It has also been won by some of the biggest names in the sport, with Marianne Vos, Emma Pooley, Anna van der Breggen and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney all featuring on its palmarès.

items.title: Visma steps down as title sponsor of Visma-Lease a Bike team
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike have confirmed that Visma will no longer be part of the team name in 2027, with the Norwegian software company stepping down from its title sponsorship role but not leaving the team completely.

Such a move has been on the cards for months, and it was first reported back in February that Visma was looking to reduce the level of its investment, but the exact nature of the relationship from 2027 was made official on Thursday.

The team announced that Visma will become a 'Founding Partner' of both men's and women's teams, in a similar move to another former title sponsor, Jumbo.

"As part of this new partnership structure, Visma will no longer serve as the team’s name partner," read a statement from the team.

"The designation of Founding Partner recognises the role Visma has played in the team’s development since 2019, a period marked by continuous innovation and fantastic sporting success."

It is not yet clear who will step in as a co-title sponsor in 2027, with team management conducting an extensive sponsorship search for much of this year. As it stands, the team has simply been registered by the name of its holding company, Yellow B, in the initial application process for 2027 UCI WorldTour and Women's WorldTour licences.

Visma began its sponsorship of the team in 2019, and its title sponsorship coincided with a hugely successful period in which the team won 10 men's Grand Tours, including all three in the same season in 2023, and the 2025 Tour de France Femmes.

“It’s fantastic that Visma is extending its partnership with our team. Visma believed in our ambitions when we started working together in 2019," said team boss Richard Plugge.

"Since then, we’ve shared moments we could only dream of back then. I’m grateful to everyone at Visma for the trust they’ve placed in us over the years. Having Visma stay with the team as a Founding Partner reflects what we’ve built together."

Visma's CEO Merete Hverven was also quoted in the announcement, explaining that the company's "strategic priorities have evolved" as it has expanded from the Nordic region into Europe and Latin America.

Rather than the title nature of the sponsorship being brought to an end, this was framed within the context of several of Visma's subsidiary brands coming on board as minor sponsors from 2027.

"This strategic evolution is reflected in the updated partnership, where several of Visma’s leading national brands across Europe, offering accounting software for SMBs, will have their logos showcased on the team jersey next season.

Those sponsors will be revealed at a later date.

items.title: Lapierre on the brink of salvation with court studying multiple offers, as a former pro cyclist 'really wants to acquire' the French bike brand
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Lapierre is among the brands which Dublin-based Quanta Capital is hoping to save after the collapse of the Accell Group, can confirm.

Last week the Sunday Times reported that a deal to acquire the French bike manufacturer, along with historic British bike brand Raleigh, had been done, but the transaction is not yet complete, according to Lapierre's Directeur Général William Perrier.

Lapierre, which supplies bikes to the Picnic-PostNL team, was founded in 1946 and has been making bikes in the French city of Dijon ever since. It was bought by Accell Group in 1996, but since the parent company’s collapse in August of this year, it has been in court supervised administration, allowing a six-month observation period from September 21 to find new investment.

"We had some offers on the table, and more recently, beginning of this week, we were in front of the court to do a check after the offers and to have a clear status [on] where we are and what we still have to work on to make it happen," Perrier told .

"I will only comment the Lapierre part, but of course Quanta is one of the candidates, but from now on the court did not take any decision.

"We are looking at it, but I don't want to promise too much, right? We are still working on having a new owner, nothing is 100% signed."

Accell, which owned a number of other cycling brands, struggled after the Covid-19 pandemic. In late July it was due to be bought by the Singapore-based DuTech Holdings, but Accell was declared bankrupt five days later, and the deal fell through, leaving its brands high and dry, though DuTech has since acquired some of Accell’s other brands.

Led by former pro cyclist Mel Sutcliffe, Quanta Capital’s interest in some of Accell’s brands was rumoured and confirmed soon after the collapse, and now it seems close to fruition.

"So there is still some discussion between all the parties to check the financing part, the social part, the overall project in order to sign the deal. But as of today, of course, Quanta is one of the potential bidders who really wants to acquire Lapierre," Perrier continued.

"But this morning [Thursday, November 26] I can tell you that it is not yet the case. There is like a lot of discussion ongoing. We are still working normally, we are still producing bikes in Dijon. We are still delivering as much as possible [to] our dealers and our final customers."

Sutcliffe declined to comment when approached by and a request for comment has since gone unanswered.

British bike brand Raleigh was acquired by Accell in 2012, but although Quanta is confirmed as being interested in the brand, with the Sunday Times reporting the deal is done, there seems little left to save.

In late September the Nottingham Post reported that a total of 43 employees had been made redundant, with only two retained, and that the company’s remaining stock had been sold to UK Bike retail chain Halfords for more than £7m.

The administrators’ report stated: "No part of the trading business was transferred as a going concern as this was ceased immediately upon our appointment." That leaves the Raleigh trademark, which is still owned by Accell and its creditors.
